The shortened expression retains that distinctive creation-to-eternity relationship and its order. It removes the intermediate dedication statement and an explicit repetition of present help, then makes the minimum case and verb changes needed to connect the surviving clauses. Individualized old whole expression plus conventional revisions; no permission inferred from English acceptance. The old whole sentence already supplies the complete architecture and its distinctive contrast: having received the saving gift, an appeal to mercy asks that the very sacrament sustaining temporal life make its recipients participants in perpetual life. Moving sacramento around its relative clause and efficias after its complement leaves that expression intact. Benignus is a real predicative addition, but it gives the same invoked merciful giver a routine graciousness qualification at the same requested act. The coordinated terminal cadence and changed placement have been assessed together: they neither replace the old contrast with another rhetorical design nor develop an additional image or clause. They remain conventional local adjustments to the preexisting expressive sentence. On this exact evidence I find a defensible nonoriginal-minor-revision basis, not merely a high similarity score or an atomized claim that individual words are free. Strongest contrary: A modern editor could argue that delaying sacramento and bringing benignus efficias to the end creates a deliberate new cadence, with benignus contributing an actual shade of meaning. Originality has a low threshold, and no complete pre1931 witness for this exact altered reading has been found within the packet search boundary. That is a genuine adverse consideration, but intentional editing and alternative word orders alone do not supply new protectable expression. Here the specific conventional qualification and routine local inversions leave the inherited sentence and its expressive contrast substantially untransformed. This is a narrow review judgment, not a legal ruling or a general license for added epithets.

after_provenance_entry.publication_evidence: CONDITIONAL POSTIMAGE ONLY: Root finite Latin decision is required. Individualized old whole expression plus conventional revisions; no permission inferred from English acceptance. The complete old prayer supplies the reception-and-renewal opening, appeal to divine clemency and antithesis between recurring ritual celebration and secured redemption. Alimonia changes the instrumental noun from sacramental draught/offering to nourishment; that lexical and semantic distinction is acknowledged, not normalized away. In this particular sentence, however, it remains an ordinary sacramental-food designation governed by the same Body-and-Blood genitives and modifying the same renovati. Moving the participle after that instrument and rearranging gerimus/devotione frequenti preserves the old linked construction. Assessed as a whole, these revisions do not develop the food term into a new comparison, add an image to the redemption petition, or recast the inherited coordination. I find the changes conventional and minor in expression, despite their real semantic nuance. The affirmative basis is the complete old composition plus that individualized judgment, not a rule that single-noun changes are always free. Strongest contrary: Alimonia can deliberately foreground nourishment where libamen foregrounds a draught or offering, and in a brief prayer even one word can make an original expressive change. The rearranged opening could therefore be alleged to be a newly fashioned presentation of eucharistic renewal. This is the strongest of the three adverse cases. It does not prevail here because the new noun functions as a routine direct label within the unchanged old instrumental phrase; the rest of the expressive coordination, including the devotion/redemption contrast, is inherited complete. The record supports a qualified affirmative under the repository presumption, not certainty that a court would decide the same way.
